sentences.text: They walked the pasture in a slow loop.
Ólafur counted.
He knew almost every sheep individually — from their ear-marks and the small differences in their faces.
Signe walked with him and helped when he asked, but mostly she watched him work.
He was very calm.
The sheep let him touch them without moving away.
By the time they had walked the full loop it was nearly ten.
The wind had risen and the cloud on the western horizon was noticeably closer.
Ólafur had counted two hundred and ninety-two sheep.
There should have been three hundred.
Eight were somewhere.
He was not too worried about seven of them — those were younger, gregarious sheep who tended to stay near the flock, and were probably in one of the folds he had not been able to see into.
But Ester was not with the flock.
And Ester was always with the flock at bad-weather times.
That was what she did.
Ólafur put his hand up to shield his eyes and looked up the ridge, above the pasture, to where the ground rose steeply into rock.
About a hundred and fifty meters up, running across the face, was a narrow ledge trail Signe had not noticed before.
"There is a small side ledge up there," Ólafur said.
"A crack in the rock, half-hidden.
There is grass on it.
Very sweet grass — a small alpine mustard grows only there.
Ester goes up sometimes to eat it.
She is the only one of the flock who knows.
She showed her mother once and her mother showed her.
She has never taken any of the others." He looked at Signe.
"If she is up there and the storm comes hard, she cannot get back down the ledge in the wet.
It is too narrow.
I am going up.
It will take an hour.
You can wait here in the shepherd's shelter" — he pointed to a small stone hut Signe had not noticed, tucked into the base of the rock face — "or you can come with me.
If you come, you follow me exactly.
You do not step where I have not stepped."
Signe thought for perhaps three seconds.
She said, "I come." Ólafur nodded.
He handed her his staff.
"You carry this.
I take the pack.
If I need it back I will tell you.
Come."
The climb up to the ledge was harder than the climb from the farm.
There was no trail, exactly — just a route Ólafur knew, following small rock steps and grass patches diagonally up the face.
He went slowly and stopped often to make sure Signe was still behind him.
He never rushed her.
The wind grew harder as they climbed.
Twice, Signe was frightened enough that she nearly asked to go back.
Both times she did not, because Ólafur was frightened too — she could see it in the concentration of his face — but Ólafur was going up anyway, because Ester was up there.
And Signe wanted to be someone who went up anyway.
About forty minutes in, they reached the ledge.
It ran across the face of the cliff for perhaps sixty meters, no wider than a person's shoulders in most places.
On one side, the rock wall.
On the other, a two-hundred-meter drop to the fjord below.
Ólafur said, quietly, "Now the important part.
You stay against the wall.
You watch every step I take.
Where I put my foot, you put yours.
Do not look down.
If the wind gusts hard, drop to your hands and knees and stay.
It will pass.
Understand?" Signe understood.
She had never in her life been more focused.
They found her about halfway along the ledge.
She was lying on her side against the rock wall, one of her back legs bent at a wrong angle.
She was breathing hard but she was alive.
When she saw Ólafur, she made a small quiet bleat and then was still.
She was too tired to move.
Ólafur crouched beside her.
He put his hand on her head.
He was quiet for a long moment.
Then he said to Signe, over his shoulder, without looking away from the sheep, "She has fallen.
She was reaching for the mustard higher up and lost her footing.
Her back leg is broken, mid-shin.
Not compound — the skin is not broken.
If I can splint it and get her down, she may recover.
If I leave her here, she will not survive tonight.
So we do not leave her."
The first heavy drops of rain began to fall.
Ólafur looked up at the sky.
He said, "We cannot get down the way we came, not in wet, not with her.
There is a summer seter — an old shepherd's hut — on the upper ridge, ten minutes further along the ledge.
My father used to sleep there when he was young.
It is still standing.
We take her there.
We wait out the storm.
We come down in the morning." He looked at Signe.
"Are you all right?" Signe said, "Yes." She said it with a small voice, but she said it.
Ólafur said, "Good.
Give me the staff.
Then take the pack."
Ólafur splinted Ester's leg quickly with two thin sticks from the pack and a length of rope.
Then he lifted her onto his shoulders in the old shepherd's carry — a way of lifting a sheep so its weight was balanced across the back and its four legs were held together in front.
Signe had seen him do this with lambs many times.
Ester was much bigger.
It was hard work.
When he stood up, he swayed slightly, and then found his balance, and then said, "Signe.
You go first.
Along the wall.
Same rules.
I follow.
Slowly." And they went.
The rain fell harder.
Somewhere across the fjord, a low thunder rolled.

Signe walked one foot at a time along the ledge, her hand against the wet rock, the old staff in the other, her uncle behind her carrying an eight-year-old ewe on his shoulders in the beginning of a mountain storm.
She was not brave, exactly.
She was determined, which was different, and which she would remember, later, as the first time in her life she had known the difference between the two.
